title: Risotto al Nero di Seppia
subtitle: black squid ink risotto from Venice
excerpt: Risotto al nero di seppia is jet-black from squid ink, with cuttlefish or squid cooked into the rice alongside white wine and a clean seafood stock. The flavour is intensely savoury and oceanic. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Risotto al nero di seppia is one of the signature dishes of Venice and the Venetian Lagoon, where cuttlefish have been caught since medieval times. The ink sac of the cuttlefish (or squid) was used as a natural dye and flavouring for pasta, risotto, and fish preparations. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), gives a version of cuttlefish cooked in its own ink as a common preparation of the Adriatic coast. The risotto version, combining the ink with white wine, stock, and the cuttlefish itself, is documented in Venetian cookbooks of the 20th century including Mirella Tenderini, La cucina veneziana (1980, Mursia).

glossaryTerms.definition: The natural black ink from the ink sac of cuttlefish or squid. It has a mild, saline, faintly oceanic flavour and turns food jet black. Available in sachets or small jars from fishmongers and good delis. Handle with care: it stains skin and surfaces.

content.text: Risotto al nero di seppia is one of the most theatrical-looking dishes in Italian cooking. The rice turns completely black from the

ink, and the cuttlefish or squid pieces sit within the risotto. The flavour is more subtle than the appearance suggests: clean, savoury, oceanic rather than fishy. A squeeze of lemon at the table lifts everything.

Squid ink sachets are available at fishmongers and good Italian delis. Wear an apron: the ink stains permanently. The mantecatura for this risotto uses only butter and no Parmesan; cheese on shellfish or cephalopod risotto is not customary in Venice.

items.prepNote: or cuttlefish, cleaned and cut into rings and tentacles
hot light fish or vegetable stock

content.text: Stir {{squid-ink}} of squid ink sachets into {{stock-fish}} of warm fish or vegetable stock. Keep warm over a low heat.

Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a wide heavy pan over a high heat. Add {{squid-cleaned}} of squid and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until lightly coloured. Remove and set aside. They will be added back later.
Reduce heat to medium. Add {{onion}} of onion and cook for 8 minutes until soft. Add {{garlic}} of garlic and cook 1 minute. Add {{arborio-rice}} of rice and toast for 1 minute.

Add {{dry-white-wine}} of wine and stir until absorbed. Begin adding the black ink-stained stock a ladle at a time, stirring and waiting for absorption between each. After 10 minutes, return the squid to the pan. Continue adding stock until the rice is cooked through with slight bite, about 18 to 20 minutes total.
Remove from heat. Stir in {{unsalted-butter}} of cold butter and beat vigorously until glossy. Season. Rest 1 minute. Serve with {{parsley-flat}} of parsley and lemon wedges.

items.cause: Either overcooked or not cooked long enough (squid needs either very short or very long cooking)
items.fix: In a risotto the squid cooks for the full 10 minutes after being returned to the pan, which is usually enough to tenderise it. If squid rings are thick, add them earlier. Cuttlefish takes longer and is more forgiving.

items.symptom: Colour is grey rather than black
items.fix: Use both sachets. The risotto should be a true, deep black when finished.

content.text: Risotto nero is a Venetian dish, tied to the lagoon and the fishing traditions of the Adriatic. It appears in the bacari (wine bars) of the Rialto and Cannaregio. The ink was once extracted from the cuttlefish by the cook; sachets make this easier, and the flavour is the same. Eaten in Venice with a glass of Soave and a view of a canal, it is as good as Italian cooking gets.
